what: 1 From Multivariate Time Series to Anomaly Routing
title: Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Routing with isoRouting: an Application to HVAC Telemetry
text: Analyzing multivariate time series physical industrial systems requires distinguishing true operational faults routine dynamic shifts across multiple coupled sensors. Turning raw sensor streams actionable diagnostics faces two fundamental hurdles: Geometric complexity: variables interact nonlinearly across shifting operating regimes Computational scalability: calibrating alert thresholds, clustering fault modes, routing live telemetry must execute rapidly across tens thousands time points. isoRouting addresses challenges within unified S4 pipeline, bridging non-parametric anomaly isolation fast, scale-free clustering, fault archetypes, threshold diagnostics streaming fault triage. Building predictive diagnostic models multivariate time series begins feature selection. standard machine learning reflex compute linear correlation matrix identify drop redundant variables. useful simple stochastic processes, linear assumption frequently breaks physical domains. industrial Internet Things (IoT) environments, example, variables governed causal, closed-loop mechanics. illustrate , load hvac_features dataset (Turin HVAC telemetry (Borda 2022)) provided isoRouting examine linear correlation across 10 telemetry channels time (timestamp) Figure 1: Global Pearson correlation heatmap (Turin HVAC Raw Telemetry) Based heatmap one tempted remove variables high correlation. However, examining raw pairwise dependencies reveals much complex geometric reality. Figure 2: Scatterplot matrix correlation-mapped backgrounds (Sampled n = 2,500) scatterplot matrix shows linear correlation inadequate measure : variables form nonlinear clusters, distinct operating modes, hard boundaries dictated mechanical limits programmed setpoints. Explicitly modeling dependencies parametric methods require prohibitive expansion interaction terms. geometric complexity isoRouting builds upon Isolation Forest algorithm (Liu et al. 2008). Rather modeling intricate structure normal operations, Isolation Forest uses recursive random partitioning isolate observations fall outside dense operational regions. standard Isolation Forest assigns anomaly score S(x)∈(0,1)S(x) \(0, 1) every timestamp, raw score vector leaves several operational questions unanswered: Feature Selection & Attribution: engineered features actively drive anomaly isolation, ones dilute upper tail anomaly scores? Threshold Calibration: set anomaly score cutoff? Fault Mode Discovery & kk-Selection: distinct physical fault types, called archetypes, exist inside anomalous tail, many clusters (kk) structurally stable? Streaming Triage & Novelty Rejection: new telemetry arrives, anomaly match known historical archetype, novel failure mode? Novelty Sub-Clustering: Among newly flagged unknown anomalies, seeing isolated spikes distinct emerging archetypes? isoRouting uses fitted Isolation Forest anomaly detector similarity engine—extracting terminal leaf memberships directly trees keep every stage exploration, clustering, live routing fast: Fast Scoring & Feature Auditing (extract_anomalies, ablate_features): tree Isolation Forest (isotree) grown small, fixed random subsample observations (sample_size, ψ=256\psi = 256) rather full time series length NN, tree construction scales 𝒪(ntψlog⁡ψ)\mathcal{O}(n_t \psi \log \psi) (ntn_t number trees) scoring scales linearly 𝒪(Nntlog⁡ψ)\mathcal{O}(N n_t \log \psi). allows users rapidly audit candidate feature sets via permutation medoid feature ablation (ablate_features()) without computational bottlenecks. Hartigan’s Dip Statistic (DD) (Hartigan Hartigan 1985) tests pairwise tail distances multimodality, indicating tail separates distinct fault clusters. Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID\text{LID}) (Amsaleg et al. 2015; Houle 2017) estimates local degrees freedom via kk-nearest neighbor distances, identifying anomalies collapse onto constrained mechanical trajectories (LID≪p\text{LID} \ll p, pp number features) rather diffuse background noise. measures minimally sensitive subset size NaN_a (e.g., DD scale-free effect size), computational speed makes practical benchmark observed values Monte Carlo null distributions (simulate_dip_control(), simulate_lid_control()). Scale-Free Clustering & Fault Archetypes (compute_distances): Instead comparing raw sensors incompatible units, isoRouting extracts Na×ntN_a \times n_t matrix terminal leaf IDs forest computes pairwise Hamming distances (fraction trees two points land different leaves). Partitioning scale-free distance matrix via divisive hierarchical clustering (DIANA (Kaufman Rousseeuw 1990)) splits broad anomalies specific fault regimes summarizes cluster medoid—actual historical observation serves cluster’s representative archetype. Fast Streaming Triage & Novelty Detection (predict_stream): Incoming observations (NnewN_{\text{new}}) scored routed comparing leaf memberships solely kk cluster medoids 𝒪(Nnewnt(log⁡ψ+k))\mathcal{O}(N_{\text{new}} n_t (\log \psi + k)) time. Custom function to calculate correlation and map it to a background color custom_scatter_bg <- function(data, mapping, ...) {   x_data <- GGally::eval_data_col(data, mapping$x)   y_data <- GGally::eval_data_col(data, mapping$y)     corr <- cor(x_data, y_data, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")     color_fun <- colorRamp(c("#f8766d", "white", "#00bfc4"))   scaled_corr <- (corr + 1) / 2     rgb_vec <- color_fun(scaled_corr)   hex_color <- rgb(rgb_vec[1], rgb_vec[2], rgb_vec[3], maxColorValue = 255)     ggplot(data, mapping) +     annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,              fill = hex_color, alpha = 0.4) +     geom_point(...) }  # 2. Generate M = 100 unconditional random 24-feature subsets (for Panel A & p-value) M <- 100L set.seed(2026) uncond_subsets <- lapply(seq_len(M), function(i) {   sample(vars_30, size = 24, replace = FALSE) })  # Supplement rare hypergeometric strata (k = 1 and k = 2) with 15 random subsets each # so Panel B displays the full stepwise dilution curve across all k in {1..6} sample_fixed_k <- function(k_target, n_reps) {   lapply(seq_len(n_reps), function(i) {     c(       sample(dwell_cols, size = k_target, replace = FALSE),       sample(vars_24, size = 24L - k_target, replace = FALSE)     )   }) }  supp_subsets <- c(sample_fixed_k(1L, 15L), sample_fixed_k(2L, 15L)) all_subsets  <- c(uncond_subsets, supp_subsets) is_uncond    <- c(rep(TRUE, M), rep(FALSE, length(supp_subsets)))  # 4. Evaluate each fixed 24-feature subset using an exact 500-tree Isolation Forest mc_workers <- if (.Platform$OS.type == "unix") n_cores else 1L  mc_all <- parallel::mclapply(seq_along(all_subsets), function(i) {   sampled_vars <- all_subsets[[i]]   n_dwell_in   <- sum(sampled_vars %in% dwell_cols)   sub_mat      <- mat_30[, sampled_vars]      iso_m <- isolation.forest(     sub_mat, ntrees = ntrees_mc, sample_size = 256,     nthreads = 1L, seed = 42, missing_action = "fail"   )   sc_m <- predict(iso_m, sub_mat, nthreads = 1L)      tibble(     iter          = i,     unconditional = is_uncond[i],     n_dwell       = factor(n_dwell_in, levels = as.character(0:6)),     tail_mass_50  = mean(sc_m >= 0.50)   ) }, mc.cores = mc_workers) |> bind_rows()  # Separate unconditional null draws (Panel A) from full stratified draws (Panel B) mc_uncond <- filter(mc_all, unconditional)  # 5. Compute exact Phipson-Smyth permutation p-value on the unconditional draws emp_pct <- 100 * mean(mc_uncond$tail_mass_50 <= obs_tail_mass_50) p_val   <- (1 + sum(mc_uncond$tail_mass_50 >= obs_tail_mass_50)) / (M + 1)  # 6. Reference point for the core 24-feature configuration (0 dwell counters) core_point_df <- tibble(   n_dwell      = factor("0", levels = as.character(0:6)),   tail_mass_50 = obs_tail_mass_50 ) library(ggplot2) library(patchwork)  # 1. Panel A: Histogram of unconditional random 24-feature subsets p_hist_mc <- ggplot(mc_uncond, aes(x = tail_mass_50 * 100)) +   geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "#0072B2", color = "white", alpha = 0.75) +   geom_vline(xintercept = obs_tail_mass_50 * 100, color = "#D55E00", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.1) +   annotate(     "text",     x = obs_tail_mass_50 * 100, y = Inf,     label = sprintf("Core 24 Set
(%.2f%%, p = %.4f)", obs_tail_mass_50 * 100, p_val),     hjust = 1.08, vjust = 1.4, fontface = "bold", color = "#D55E00", size = 3.5   ) +   theme_bw(base_size = 11) +   labs(     title    = "A. Null Distribution of Tail Mass (d = 24)",     subtitle = sprintf("%d random 24-of-30 subsets (ntrees = %d)", M, ntrees_mc),     x        = "Upper-Tail Mass (% Score >= 0.50)",     y        = "Number of Random Subsets"   )  # 2. Panel B: Stepwise Dilution by Number of Included Mode Dwell Counters (0 to 6) p_dwell_effect <- ggplot(mc_all, aes(x = n_dwell, y = tail_mass_50 * 100)) +   geom_boxplot(fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.35, outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) +   geom_jitter(aes(shape = unconditional), width = 0.15, alpha = 0.7, color = "#2C7BB6") +   scale_shape_manual(     values = c(`TRUE` = 16, `FALSE` = 2),     labels = c(`TRUE` = "Unconditional (Panel A)", `FALSE` = "Stratified (k = 1, 2)"),     name   = NULL   ) +   geom_point(     data = core_point_df,     aes(x = n_dwell, y = tail_mass_50 * 100),     color = "#D55E00", size = 4.5, shape = 18   ) +   annotate(     "text",     x = "0", y = obs_tail_mass_50 * 100,     label = "Core 24",     hjust = -0.25, vjust = 0.5, fontface = "bold", color = "#D55E00", size = 3.4   ) +   scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +   theme_bw(base_size = 11) +   theme(legend.position = "bottom") +   labs(     title    = "B. Impact of Mode Dwell Counters",     subtitle = "Tail mass vs. dwell counter count at fixed d = 24",     x        = "Mode Dwell Counters Included (d = 24)",     y        = "Upper-Tail Mass (% Score >= 0.50)"   )  (p_hist_mc | p_dwell_effect) +   plot_layout(guides = "collect") &   theme(legend.position = "bottom")

code: library(dplyr) library(tidyr)  moisture_gaps_eda <- hvac_valid |>   arrange(timestamp) |>   select(timestamp, rh_return, rh_supply, t_supply, t_return, t_saturation) |>   mutate(     humidity_delta = rh_supply - rh_return,     supply_margin  = t_supply - t_saturation,     return_margin  = t_return - t_saturation   ) |>   filter(!is.na(humidity_delta) & !is.na(supply_margin) & !is.na(return_margin))  moisture_long <- moisture_gaps_eda |>   pivot_longer(     cols      = c(humidity_delta, supply_margin, return_margin),     names_to  = "metric",     values_to = "value"   ) |>   mutate(     metric = factor(       metric,       levels = c("humidity_delta", "supply_margin", "return_margin"),       labels = c(         "Humidity Delta (rh_supply - rh_return) [%]",         "Supply Margin (t_supply - t_saturation) [\u00B0C]",         "Return Margin (t_return - t_saturation) [\u00B0C]"       )     )   ) library(ggplot2)  ggplot(moisture_long, aes(x = value, fill = metric)) +   geom_histogram(bins = 150, color = "black", alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0.1) +   facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free", ncol = 1) +   scale_fill_manual(values = c("#0868ac", "#7bccc4", "#43a2ca")) +   theme_bw(base_size = 12) +   labs(     title    = "Moisture Gaps and Saturation Margins",     subtitle = "Distributions of engineered humidity and saturation relationships",     x        = "Difference",     y        = "Frequency"   ) +   theme(     legend.position  = "none",     strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),     strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold")   ) library(dplyr) library(tidyr)  # 1.
